passage:
Monday. "I'm bored," said Sumit, mid-homework, and before the sigh was finished Vasudha had put the tablet in his hands. Ten minutes of quiet. She felt like a good mother.
Wednesday. Same sigh, same tablet. That night Sumit was cranky when she took it back, and Vasudha wondered what she was teaching him.
Saturday. "I'm bored." She said, "Hmm. Tell me what you come up with," and went on chopping onions, her heart thumping a little. He whined for a few minutes, then vanished. She found him on the balcony with a cardboard-box city and a story to go with it.

qa.q: What did Sumit make on the balcony?
qa.a: A cardboard-box city with a story to go with it.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling on Wednesday night as she took the tablet back?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and doubtful, wondering what she was teaching Sumit.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do on Saturday instead of handing over the tablet?
qa.a: She asked Sumit to tell her what he came up with and kept chopping onions, letting him whine for a few minutes.

qa.q: What might Sumit have felt when Vasudha did not hand over the tablet?
qa.a: Annoyed and stuck at first, since he whined, and then curious and busy once he started on the box city.

grounding: A parent who instantly hands over a tablet learns what a short unrescued wait can produce.

passage:
Mehak beta, this old mother Hafsa will tell you what she learned from her son Zaid. When he was nine and said "I'm bored," I handed him the tablet before he finished the sentence. It seemed kind.
Then, one wet Sunday, the tablet was at the repair shop, and Zaid moaned all morning that he would die of boredom. I nearly ran to my sister to borrow hers. But I was tired, so I let him moan.
By afternoon he had emptied a drawer of matchboxes and built a whole city with roads, and he made me the mayor. So when you feel like filling your little one's silence, try five minutes first.

qa.q: Where was the tablet on the wet Sunday?
qa.a: It was at the repair shop.

qa.q: What did Hafsa feel as Zaid moaned that he would die of boredom?
qa.a: Tempted to rescue him and tired. She nearly ran to borrow a tablet, then let him moan.

qa.q: What choice did Hafsa make that changed the day?
qa.a: She let Zaid moan instead of borrowing a tablet, and by afternoon he had built a matchbox city.

qa.q: How might Zaid have felt when he made Hafsa the mayor?
qa.a: Proud and playful, since he built the city himself and got to give his mother a role in it.

grounding: An elder recalls handing a child a tablet at each complaint of boredom and what a short unrescued wait produced.

passage:
On the twelve-hour train to Amritsar, Usha watched her nephew Amandeep swipe the tablet from the moment they sat down. Every time he said "bored" at home, his parents handed it straight over; she had seen it a hundred times.
Near Ambala the battery died, and the charger was in the other suitcase, in the luggage van. Amandeep's face crumpled. "Masi, I'm SO bored. Do something!"
Usha's hand went to her own phone. Then she stopped. "Hmm. We've got a window."
He sulked for fifteen minutes, forehead pressed to the glass. Then: "That's the fourth buffalo with a white spot." He borrowed her pen and started a tally on a paper napkin. By Ludhiana it had columns for buffaloes, tractors and people waving, and he'd invented points for each.

qa.q: Where was the charger?
qa.a: In the other suitcase, in the luggage van.

qa.q: Why did Usha stop reaching for her own phone?
qa.a: Usha felt tempted to rescue him but held back, sensing he needed a chance to fill the boredom himself after years of the tablet being handed over.

qa.q: What could Amandeep's parents learn from the train ride?
qa.a: That a short wait without rescuing, instead of handing over the tablet straight away, can lead him to invent something.

qa.q: What was the journey like for Amandeep after the battery died?
qa.a: At first he was miserable and sulky, then absorbed and proud, scoring buffaloes, tractors and waving people.

grounding: Shows an observer who has watched a child always rescued from boredom by a tablet, and what happens when rescue is withheld.

passage:
Every evening in their Thane flat it went the same way. Omkar would flop on the sofa and say, "Papa, I'm bored," and Madhav, tired from work, would hand over the tablet within seconds. It was kind. It was also easy.
Then the tablet went for repair for a week. On Monday Omkar followed Madhav around for half an hour, groaning. Madhav nearly handed over his own phone. He didn't.
By Wednesday Madhav came home to find the dining table turned into a car workshop: toy cars in a line, a shoebox garage, price tags in Omkar's wobbly writing. "Papa, you have to bring your car for service."
Madhav sat down and let his son explain the repair to him. He couldn't remember when he'd last seen Omkar this busy with his own idea.

qa.q: What did Omkar turn the dining table into?
qa.a: A car workshop, with toy cars, a shoebox garage and price tags.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling as Omkar explained the repair?
qa.a: Madhav felt surprised and moved, realising he couldn't remember Omkar being this busy with his own idea.

qa.q: What could Madhav do when the tablet comes back?
qa.a: When Omkar says "I'm bored", Madhav could wait a while before offering it, leaving room for games like the workshop.

qa.q: What was Monday like for Omkar?
qa.a: Omkar felt bored and restless, groaning and following his father around for half an hour.

grounding: Shows a parent noticing that instantly handing over a tablet had kept his child from inventing his own play.

passage:
"Mumma, I'm bored."
Vidya reached for the tablet on the shelf without looking up from her tea. "Here, beta."
Parveen, her neighbour, watched nine-year-old Kiaan disappear into the screen. "That was fast."
"If I don't, he whines for an hour."
"Does he? Last Sunday at my place the tablet was dead. He whined for maybe ten minutes."
"And then?"
"Then he built a ramp out of my cookbooks and raced bottle caps down it. Made me the judge."
Vidya put down her cup. "He never does that here."
"Maybe he's never had to."
Vidya was quiet. Then she said, "Next time, I'll try ten minutes."

qa.q: What did Kiaan build at Parveen's place?
qa.a: A ramp out of her cookbooks, to race bottle caps down.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when she said "He never does that here"?
qa.a: Vidya felt surprised and a little uneasy, seeing that her quick rescue may be why Kiaan doesn't invent games at home.

qa.q: What small step did Vidya decide on?
qa.a: Next time Kiaan says he is bored, wait ten minutes before handing over the tablet.

qa.q: How does Parveen see Vidya's habit?
qa.a: Parveen sees it as kind but quick, having noticed that Kiaan whined only ten minutes when there was no tablet.

grounding: Shows an observer pointing out a parent's habit of instantly handing over a tablet, and a short unrescued wait yielding creativity.

passage:
I'm Vikas, Gargi's Papa, and for a long time I handed her the tablet the moment she said "I'm bored." It seemed kind. It was quiet.
Then one Sunday I noticed something. She didn't even want the tablet; she wanted the boredom to stop. The second it was in her hands, her face went blank.
So the next time she said it, I said, "Hmm. That's a hard feeling. You'll figure something out," and went back to cooking.
She sulked. She followed me around. She lay on the floor saying "Papa, PLEASE." I nearly gave in.
Twenty minutes later it went quiet. I peeked. She had lined up all her stuffed toys and was holding a school, with a register and a tiny chalkboard she'd drawn on cardboard.
Now I wait a bit before rescuing her. She usually rescues herself.

qa.q: What did Gargi make her chalkboard from?
qa.a: She drew a tiny chalkboard on cardboard.

qa.q: What did Vikas realise about handing Gargi the tablet?
qa.a: Vikas felt uneasy when he noticed her face go blank, realising she only wanted the boredom to stop, not the tablet itself.

qa.q: What change did Vikas make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He named the feeling, didn't rush to fill it and waited, which gave Gargi room to invent her own game.

qa.q: What was the wait like for Gargi?
qa.a: Gargi felt frustrated and bored at first, sulking and pleading, then absorbed and happy running her toy school.

grounding: A parent notices that rescuing a child from boredom with a tablet teaches outside filling, and a short wait brings creativity.
